newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's VIP hostages approach gloomy Christmas Eve.
newsitem.headline: Peru's VIP hostages approach gloomy Christmas Eve.

text.p: More than 140 hostages faced a miserable Christmas Eve in Lima on Tuesday as defiant Marxist rebels kept them captive for the seventh day of their showdown with a shocked Peruvian government.

The men received Christmas cakes from the Red Cross, but had little else to cheer them as they prepared to spend the holiday under the guns of 20 heavily armed guerrillas from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) instead of with their familes.

Red Cross spokesman Steve Andersen told reporters that aid workers would send "something special" in the evening for the men inside the Japanese ambassador's residence, which the MRTA seized during a cocktail party last on Tuesday.
Latin Americans traditionally celebrate Christmas with a family meal on the night of December 24.

One Peruvian bishop, Miguel Irizar from Lima's neighbouring port of Callao, urged a nationwide suspension of Christmas celebrations. "While we are not sure of resolving this problem peacefully, we cannot have parties or be frivolous," he said.
Peruvians, whose Christmas preparations have been overshadowed by the hostage drama, speculated endlessly over what would be the next step.
Following the release on Sunday night of 225 hostages as a goodwill gesture, the rebels have kept an ominous silence.
In Hamburg, Germany, however, a man claiming to be their international spokesman said the MRTA would never surrender.

"Effectively, what the government of President (Albert) Fujimori is asking is that the group ... gives up," said Isaac Velzaco in a television interview with Cable News Network. "The word surrender or capitulation is not in the vocabulary of the Tupac Amaru soldier."
Earlier on Monday, a woman claiming to be Velazco's wife, Norma Velazco, called a Paraguayan radio station from Hamburg claiming the MRTA was planning more attacks.

Police sources in Lima concurred, telling Reuters they believed another clandestine MRTA commando unit was at large in the Peruvian capital and could strike if dialogue breaks down. "If (police) storm the embassy, it is possible they will start car bomb attacks or other sabotage," one source said.

On the government side, a Peruvian crack commando team was standing by to storm the residence if necessary as a last resort. However, Fujimori has told the rebels he would not use force and would consider a peaceful "way out" if they laid down their arms and gave up all their hostages.
His plea, and later ones from U.S. President Bill Clinton and Pope John Paul to release the captives, seems to have fallen on deaf ears.
The government kept electricity and telephone services to the building cut on Tuesday, but water was expected to be restored later in the day.
Overnight, a small group of Peruvians held a candlelit vigil close to the residence.
"The solidarity has been shown in many ways and now more than ever we pray to the Virgin Mary to soften the hearts of the captors and let all the hostages out," one woman at the ceremony said.

Red Cross officials, who are mediating the crisis, said no negotiator had been in since Sunday, although there were rumours of talks behind the scenes including a possible option to give the rebels exile in Cuba.

The MRTA fighters seized the residence a week ago during a posh reception to commemorate Japanese Emperor Akihito's birthday, taking more than 500 hostages. Many -- including all the American, British and German captives -- have been freed.

But the rebels were still holding President Alberto Fujimori's brother, dozens of top Peruvian governnment officials, about 30 high-ranking Japanese businessmen and diplomats, and some Latin American ambassadors.

The Red Cross was trying to establish the identity of seven of the 225 freed on Sunday night whose names did not match those on a master list of captives to be freed. One theory in local media was that an MRTA rebel might have slipped out.
Remaining captives in the residence -- and waiting hordes of journalists from around the world -- could face a long stay.

The rebels, led by Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, a textile worker turned revolutionary, have demanded that the government set free jailed MRTA comrades before ending the siege, but Fujimori has flatly refused.
Reflecting the grief felt in Japan, Emperor Akihito cancelled all official birthday celebrations on Monday, while Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto tracked the crisis from a special war room.

"I think it will take time (to resolve the crisis)," Hashimoto told reporters on Tuesday shortly after speaking by telephone with Peru's Fujimori. "We are in for a long haul, even if the New Year holiday is ruined."
Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda called off a visit to South Korea on Tuesday and said "difficult judgments" were now needed to resolve the crisis in Peru.
Most Peruvians, long tired of rebel violence, have backed Fujimori's hard line against the rebels, but worries were growing about conditions inside the besieged compound.
Released hostage Victor Lucero, a doctor, said captives had developed at least eight cases of an eye infection because of the unhygienic conditions. Outbreaks of diarrhoea have also been reported.
